horsehair.types: Horsehair is graded by source, length and color. Tail hair is longer and is used for weaving and bows; mane and body hair is shorter and goes into curled upholstery stuffing and brushes. Weavers report white tail hair at roughly 20 inches (about 50 cm) and black or brown hair up to about 25 inches, which sets the width of woven haircloth. Bow makers prefer tail hair from stallions in cold climates such as Mongolia and Siberia, dressed repeatedly to remove kinked or thick hairs; white hair is standard for violin, viola and cello bows. Curled hair is sold by grade and hair content, and synthetic monofilament horsehair braid is a separate, non-hair product.
horsehair.fabrics: Haircloth is woven with a single horse tail hair as each weft pick on a cotton, silk or linen warp, so fabric widths are limited to roughly 70 cm or less. It comes in plain, satin and patterned weaves for chair seats, headboards, wall panels and luxury upholstery. Hair canvas interlinings stiffen the chests and lapels of tailored jackets. Curled mane hair fills traditional sprung upholstery and mattresses. A violin bow carries a flat ribbon of roughly 150 to 200 tail hairs, rosined to grip the string. Horsehair also appears in brushes, fishing lines, jewelry and millinery.
horsehair.quality: Genuine haircloth has a crisp, slightly glossy surface where individual hair ends are visible at the selvedges, and a burn test on a loose weft end gives a hair smell and brittle ash rather than a melted bead. Width is a cue: horsehair fabric wider than the longest tail hairs is suspect. For bow hair, look for even, straight hairs without kinks and ask whether it is stallion hair and from which region. For upholstery, curled hair should spring back strongly when compressed; hair mixed with plant fiber or synthetic fill is cheaper. Millinery braid labeled horsehair is usually nylon or polyester.
pros: Haircloth is extremely durable and resists crushing and wear on seats.
Stiff, springy hairs give tailored interlinings and upholstery lasting shape.
Bow hair has a scale structure that holds rosin and grips strings.
Tail hair can be collected from living horses without harm.
cons: Haircloth widths are narrow, which limits pattern layout and raises cost.
Stiff hair ends can poke through covers and scratch skin.
Bow hair wears and stretches, so regular players need rehairing every few months.
Old horsehair stuffing attracts moths and carpet beetles and can harbor dust.
horsehair.impact: Horsehair is a by-product: tail hair is trimmed from living horses or recovered at slaughter, depending on the supply chain, and haircloth weavers such as the long-established English mill John Boyd Textiles state that they use tail hair from live horses. Volumes are small and published environmental data are scarce, so no quantified footprint is available. Processing uses washing, degreasing, sometimes bleaching, and dyeing. Welfare questions concern trimming practices and slaughter conditions in supplying countries, which buyers can only check through supplier information. Curled hair stuffing is durable and can be reclaimed and re-curled by upholsterers, extending product life compared with foam.
horsehair.care: Vacuum haircloth upholstery with a soft brush attachment and wipe with a barely damp cloth; avoid soaking, which can loosen hairs and stain the warp. Test any spot cleaner on a hidden area. Keep furniture out of strong sun, which fades dyed hair and dries the warp. Hair canvas in tailored jackets should be dry cleaned or professionally pressed, not washed. Bows need rosin, loosened hair after playing, and clean hands; avoid touching the hair. Store bows away from heat and humidity swings and watch for bow bugs (carpet beetle larvae) in cases. The product label governs.
faq: Is horsehair braid in hats real horsehair?

Usually not. Most millinery braid sold as horsehair is nylon or polyester monofilament. A burn test on a single strand separates them: synthetic melts to a hard bead, while real hair chars with a burning-hair smell.
Why are violin bows strung with horsehair?

Horse tail hair has a scaled surface that holds rosin, which makes the hair grip and release the string to set it vibrating. A bow uses roughly 150 to 200 hairs, and bow makers favor stallion hair from cold climates for strength.
How often should a bow be rehaired?

String shops commonly advise about every 6 to 12 months for regular players and more often for daily professional use. Signs include lost hairs, poor grip even after rosining, and uneven hair tension.
Why is horsehair fabric so narrow?
Each weft pick is a single tail hair, so the cloth can be no wider than the usable length of the hair, roughly 70 cm or less. Wider fabrics labeled horsehair usually contain other fibers.
notable: John Boyd Textiles has woven horsehair fabric in Castle Cary, England, since 1837, using mechanical looms developed around 1870 that pick one hair at a time.
In hand weaving of haircloth, a child traditionally sat in the loom to pass single hairs to the weaver.
White tail hair tends to be shorter than black or brown hair, so white haircloth is narrower.
